Title: The Cartographer of Small Hours

Every night at 3:07 a.m., the lighthouse keeper named Wren climbed the stairs of an empty lighthouse on a cliff that belonged to no country, and she drew the coastline from memory.

By morning the map was wrong. Not obviously wrong — the harbors were where harbors belonged, the reefs sat in shallow water. But a mile north of the pier where the fishing boats slept, she had drawn an island. It had a name in her handwriting: TERN.

"This one," she said aloud, "is for you."

The island had been there every year of Wren's life, a low green smudge on the horizon that the fog swallowed and returned. The maps in the harbor office called it a rendering error, a trick of light on the water. The old captain of the fishing fleet called it patience.

Wren had been eight when her brother, Tomas, rowed out to look for terns — the small birds that nested on the island in summer, the ones that followed the boats home in flocks of silver. He never came back. The search boats found his skiff drifting with its oars shipped, and the sea kept its counsel.

Every year on the anniversary, Wren took the rowboat out at first light, circled where the island should be, and came home with the salt drying white on her hands.

Then the winter the government of the coastal union began buying the cliffs for a shipping terminal. Surveyors came with orange flags and laser tripods, and the map of the lighthouse man — a chain of coordinates, updated weekly — began to include the smudge of green. A harbor, they wrote. Suitable.

Wren looked at the printout for a long time. Then she went up the stairs, unlocked the lantern room, and did not come down.

At 3:07 that night, she drew the island larger. She gave it two cliffs. She gave it a grove of wind-bent pines. She drew the terns as small Vs over the headland, and a boat drawn toward them by a current that did not exist.

At dawn the surveyor climbed with her and found the work finished, the ink dry, the window open to the salt air.

"The shipping lane passes within a mile of the coordinates," he said. "Your island will be under the concrete by spring."

"Yes," said Wren. "It will."

And the terns came back that April, thousands of them, screaming over the half-built terminal, over the cranes, over the foundation piers — flying, always flying, toward the place where a boy had once rowed out alone to find them, and where, at last, an island waited.

---

By morning the map was wrong. Not obviously; harbors were where harbors belonged, reefs sat in shallow water. But north of the pier, she had drawn an island. It had a name in her handwriting: TERN. "This one," she said, "is for you."

The island had been there every year of her life, a low green smudge on the horizon the fog swallowed and returned. Harbor office maps called it a rendering error. The old captain of the fishing fleet called it patience.

Wren had been eight when her brother Tomas rowed out to find terns. He never came back. The search boats found his skiff adrift, its oars shipped, and the sea kept its counsel.

Then came the winter the union bought the cliffs for a shipping terminal. Surveyors arrived with orange flags, and the weekly map of coordinates began to include the smudge of green. A harbor, they wrote. Suitable.

Then she climbed the tower, unlocked the lantern room, and did not come down.

At 3:07 she drew the island larger: two cliffs, a grove of wind-bent pines, the terns as small Vs over the headland, a boat drawn toward them by a current that did not exist.

At dawn the surveyor found her there, ink dry.

"The shipping lane passes within a mile of those coordinates," he said. "Your island will be under concrete by spring."

"Yes," said Wren. "It will."

And the terns came back that April, screaming over the half-built terminal, over the cranes, over the foundation piers, flying always toward the place where a boy had once rowed out alone to find them, and where an island waited.
